data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference smuggles induction back in because acting on corroboration functionally requires assuming the future will resemble the past.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If one can formulate a non-inductive principle of rational action (e.g., critical rationalism) that justifies the preference.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference is purely aesthetic or psychological and not epistemic.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'future resemblance' assumption is rejected but the preference remains via a different logical route.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism is 'pragmatic induction'. Even if Popper verbally denies probability, the act of preferring Theory A over Theory B for future application entails a belief that A's past survival is relevant to its future performance. This relevance is the definition of induction. Without the hidden premise that 'what worked before will work again,' the preference is arbitrary. Thus, Popper's system collapses into a disguised form of inductivism where 'corroboration' is just a synonym for 'high inductive support'.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
